A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Video Prediction Policy work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: V1 reports original CALVIN, MetaWorld, Panda and dexterous-hand evaluations, together with video-prediction results and ablations.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports additional component ablations, latency measurements, tool-use outcomes and generalization case studies.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 replaces features from one selected diffusion-model layer with interpolated, channel-concatenated features from multiple upsampling layers. This changes the conditioning representation, while retaining the two-stage training process, Video Former and diffusion action head. The inverse-dynamics terminology does not establish a separate new algorithm.

E1.justification: The training dataset families, CALVIN ABC-to-D, MetaWorld-50 and both robot platforms remain. V2 adds spoon-use evaluation within the existing dexterous-manipulation domain. Tool use overall is not new: v1 already demonstrates hammer, drill and pipette tasks.

E2.justification: CALVIN Table 1 adds Vidman and RoboUniview, removes the 3D Diffuser Actor row, and drops MDT from the 10%-data comparison. Full-data MDT and the other established comparators remain. MetaWorld, real-world and video-prediction comparator sets are unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported VC-1 fine-tuning data change from CALVIN to VPP's video mixture. Main-text dexterous trajectory counts change from 3,000 to 4,000, although appendix counts remain approximately 2,500 and 2,476, leaving the actual data expansion unresolved. V2 also specifies ten evaluations per tool task and introduces component latency comparisons.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands diagnostic evidence with ablations removing CALVIN video pretraining, the entire Video Former and feature aggregation, plus prediction-versus-execution case studies on unseen tasks. Existing single-view, temporal-attention and two-step-denoising ablations remain. V1's joint layer/noise sweep is replaced by separate appendix summaries in Tables 10–11.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without training-seed replication counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new tool-task rollout counts extend evaluation sample-size reporting rather than introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: CALVIN VPP average length changes from 4.29 to 4.33 alongside the aggregation revision. Substantial new result groups include component scores of 3.31, 3.86 and 3.60, latency comparisons of approximately 140 versus 450 ms, and tool-use success rates averaging 0.68 for VPP versus 0.23 for Susie. MetaWorld results, Bridge FVD and existing real-world category scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 changes the mathematical definition of the conditioning representation to interpolated and concatenated multilayer features. V1's separate weighted dexterous-action loss, Equation 8, is omitted from v2's exposition; this alone does not establish changed implementation. Diffusion preliminaries remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The central predictive-representation contribution remains. V2 removes the explicit first-use novelty claim and emphasizes implicit inverse dynamics and transfer with few demonstrations. Abstract headline advantages change from 28.1% to 18.6% for CALVIN and from 28.8% to 31.6% for dexterous manipulation; comparison coverage also changes.

C2.justification: V2 expands the generalization explanation: pretrained video models predict unfamiliar scenarios, while the policy tracks predicted robot motion without needing to model new objects or backgrounds. Section 5.3 connects this interpretation to new case studies. It also adds interpretations of the Video Former's efficiency and multilayer aggregation benefits.

D1.justification: V2 adds encoder-processing details, including VAE feature dimensions and resampling to 256 tokens, and states that code is in supplementary material. Reported video-training time changes from two to two–three days. It omits the 300M/20M component parameter counts and weighted hand-loss description. Dataset-mixture and architecture/hyperparameter tables are retained unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds related work including Vidman, RoboUniview, IGOR and Prediction with Action, while removing citations such as OpenVLA and RDT-1B. It explicitly distinguishes VPP from Vidman's lack of downstream video-model fine-tuning and withdraws the first-use claim. The main related-work categories remain intact.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are substantially rewritten around implicit inverse dynamics, and the numbered contribution list is removed. Experimental setup, training and comparison discussions are reorganized; Section 5.2 becomes a focused ablation section. Prediction-quality discussion moves to Appendix B, and supplementary sections are reorganized as A–C.

P2.justification: V2 removes the original overview figure, redraws the motivation and architecture diagrams, replaces the real-world bar chart with a table, and adds a generalization figure and latency column. The layer/noise plot becomes appendix tables. Appendix prose changes to a single-column layout, with retained video visualizations relocated and rearranged.

improvement.justification: Component and latency controls in Table 4 and detailed tool-use comparisons in Table 7 provide useful evidence absent from v1, modestly strengthening support for the design and capabilities. Reporting problems limit the gain: v2's abstract gives an 18.6% CALVIN advantage over RoboUniview, while its introduction gives 41.5% against GR-1 and Section 5.1 retains the old 3.35 baseline. Unreconciled dexterous data counts and omitted loss details also weaken reproducibility.
